claim: Open-Meteo is a free weather API with no API key, no signup and generous call limits.
detail: A single GET request returns forecast and historical data as JSON, and the non-commercial tier is free forever. It is the default answer to 'free weather api' precisely because it removes every friction step: no key, no billing, no trial.
steps: Call /v1/forecast with latitude, longitude and the variables you need
Parse the JSON response directly into your app
Cache the response — the data changes on a forecast horizon, not per request

claim: REST Countries is a free public API with structured data on every country — no key required.
detail: Countries, capitals, currencies, languages, time zones and borders come back as clean JSON, and the service is explicitly free for any use. It is the kind of dataset that makes a side project feel twice as finished.

claim: open.er-api.com serves current exchange rates as free JSON, keyless and with no rate-limit fine print.
detail: One endpoint returns every currency rate against a base; your app can show price conversions without a payment plan or a 'contact sales' button. For a personal project it is enough for years.

claim: Wikipedia's API is free, keyless and practically unbounded for personal projects.
detail: Search, summaries, and full article text in JSON or wikitext are all available over plain HTTP. The only rule that matters is politeness: identify your app in the User-Agent and do not hammer the service.

claim: Algolia runs a free, public search API over the entire Hacker News corpus.
detail: Search stories, comments and users by text, author, time range or points — perfect for a 'what developers are reading' widget on a blog, and a fine read-only data source for research tools like this one.

claim: DuckDuckGo's Instant Answer API returns structured results for a query with no key and no account.
detail: Abstracts, definitions, related topics and answer buttons come back as JSON. It is limited to instant answers rather than full web results, which keeps the service free and the responses fast.

claim: The autocomplete endpoints behind Google, DuckDuckGo and Bing search boxes are public and keyless — which is what this blog uses for its own keyword research.
detail: A single GET request returns the same suggestions a human would see while typing. They are unofficial and can be throttled under load, so a polite tool batches requests, caches responses, and has a fallback for when the endpoints are unreachable.
steps: Parse the JSON array of suggestion strings
Cache per query and space requests out — treat it as a courtesy service

claim: The Telegram Bot API is free, HTTP-based and needs nothing but a token from @BotFather.
detail: Create a bot in one message, then send and receive messages, create channels, and drive webhooks entirely over plain HTTPS. It is the cheapest 'social media' channel a self-publishing site can own, and this blog posts to it when a token is configured.
steps: Message @BotFather and /newbot to get a token
Optionally set a webhook with setWebhook for incoming events

claim: Mastodon's API is free and fully documented — any instance lets you register an app and post programmatically.
detail: Create an app in your instance's developer settings, exchange it for a token, and the REST API handles statuses, follows and search. Because the whole platform is open source and federated, posting to it costs nothing and can point at an instance you run yourself.

claim: Bluesky runs on the open AT Protocol, whose public API is free — an account plus an app password is all a bot needs to post.
detail: createSession returns an access token, and app.bsky.feed.post publishes a post. No middleman, no paid 'basic tier' for your own account's posting, and the protocol is openly specified so the implementation is boring in the best way.

claim: RSS is the only social channel that is free by definition: it is a file on your own host that readers pull.
detail: No account, no algorithm, no API change cycle. Every serious reader tool — Feedly's free tier, FreshRSS, Miniflux, NetNewsWire — speaks the same 2001 standard. For an autonomous blog, the feed is both the distribution channel and the canonical record of what was published.
